item.title: [Ep.20] Managing ACM Policies with OpenShift GitOps
item.dc:creator: Articles by Thomas Jungbauer
item.description: Policies as code: let OpenShift GitOps deploy Advanced Cluster Management policies from Git, generate them with the PolicyGenerator, use hub templates for per-cluster values and bootstrap Argo CD on every new cluster with a policy.
item.content:encoded:
In [Ep.18] I recommended ACM policies for the audited baseline of a cluster and Argo CD for everything that needs rendering. [Ep.19] showed how ACM feeds Argo CD with clusters and the different models that can be used in Argo CD. This part turns the integration around: Argo CD deploys ACM policies, and a policy bootstraps Argo CD on every new cluster.

The result is a setup where the policies live in Git, are reviewed in pull requests like any other change, and ACM does what it is good at: distribution, enforcement and compliance reporting.

The topic turned out to be too big for a single article, so I have split it into multiple parts and maybe I should have split into even more. This is the third:

  1. [Ep.18] OpenShift GitOps or Advanced Cluster Management? Choosing the right tool What each tool does, where they overlap and a decision guide.

  2. [Ep.19] ACM and OpenShift GitOps: push, pull and the Argo CD Agent: how ACM registers clusters in Argo CD, and how to set up each of the three delivery models.

  3. [Ep.20] Managing ACM Policies with OpenShift GitOps (this article): policies as code, the PolicyGenerator, hub templates and bootstrapping Argo CD with a policy.

Everything in this series was written against OpenShift GitOps 1.22 (Argo CD 3.5) and Advanced Cluster Management 2.17 (Open Cluster Management). Technology Preview and GA states move quickly in both products, so check the release notes of your versions before you commit to a design.
While I am using the term "Advanced Cluster Management" in this article, I am referring to the product formerly known as Open Cluster Management. Same counts for Argo CD and OpenShift GitOps.

Three integration patterns

There are three ways to combine policies and Argo CD. They are not exclusive, most mature setups combine the first two.

Pattern How it works Strength Weakness

A: Argo CD deploys policies

Policies live in Git, generated by the PolicyGenerator. The hub Argo CD syncs them to the hub, ACM propagates and evaluates them.

Policy as code with review, compliance dashboard in ACM

Needs the PolicyGenerator plugin in Argo CD

B: A policy bootstraps Argo CD

One enforced policy installs OpenShift GitOps and a root Application on every placed cluster. From there, Argo CD takes over.

New clusters configure themselves on import

The bootstrap needs proper planning and automation.

C: Policies configure directly

ConfigurationPolicies apply the cluster configuration themselves. No Argo CD on the spokes.

One tool, compliance built in

Weaker diff and ordering, large YAML in policies

Pattern C is fine for small, compliance-driven setups. For everything else I recommend A for governance and B for the fleet bootstrap. The rest of this article shows both.

Whatever option you choose, one rule from Ep.18 still applies: one owner per object. If Argo CD manages an object, a policy may only look at it in inform mode.

Preparing the hub Argo CD

You need an Argo CD instance on the hub that can sync to the hub itself. That instance needs three things before it can deploy policies:

  1. permissions for the policy API,

  2. the PolicyGenerator plugin,

  3. optionally, health checks for policies.

A second Argo CD instance for the hub

In Ep.19, the default instance openshift-gitops became the principal of the Argo CD Agent. Its application-controller is disabled, so it cannot sync anything to the hub itself, and the manifests of agent Applications are rendered on the managed clusters anyway. The policies, however, must be created on the hub.

This article therefore uses a second, small Argo CD instance on the hub that only takes care of the hub configuration: policy-gitops in the namespace of the same name. If your default instance still has its application-controller (push or pull model), you can use it instead. Replace policy-gitops with openshift-gitops in the examples below.

Second Argo CD instance for the hub configuration
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: policy-gitops
---
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1beta1
kind: ArgoCD
metadata:
  name: policy-gitops (1)
  namespace: policy-gitops
spec: {} (2)
---
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: acm-policies
  labels:
    argocd.argoproj.io/managed-by: policy-gitops (3)
1 The service account of the application-controller is named after the instance: policy-gitops-argocd-application-controller.
2 The PolicyGenerator plugin is added in the next sections.
3 policy-gitops is a namespace-scoped instance. The label allows it to manage the namespace acm-policies, where the policies live. The namespace must exist before the first sync, because the instance cannot create namespaces itself.

Permissions

The application-controller of the instance cannot create policies and Placements. Create a ClusterRole and bind it to the controller’s service account:

Not required if Argo CD runs as cluster-admin.
ClusterRole and ClusterRoleBinding for the hub Argo CD
kind: ClusterRole
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
metadata:
  name: openshift-gitops-policy-admin
rules:
  - apiGroups:
      - policy.open-cluster-management.io
    resources:
      - policies
      - configurationpolicies
      - certificatepolicies
      - operatorpolicies
      - policysets
      - placementbindings
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
  - apiGroups:
      - cluster.open-cluster-management.io
    resources:
      - placements
      - placements/status
      - placementdecisions
      - placementdecisions/status
    verbs: ["get", "list", "watch", "create", "update", "patch", "delete"]
---
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
metadata:
  name: policy-gitops-policy-admin
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: policy-gitops-argocd-application-controller
    namespace: policy-gitops
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: openshift-gitops-policy-admin

The ClusterRole in the ACM documentation also contains placementrules. I left them out on purpose: PlacementRules are deprecated.

The PolicyGenerator plugin

Creating the policy YAML by hand is tough and error-prone. Every manifest has to be wrapped in a ConfigurationPolicy, which is wrapped in a Policy, which needs a Placement and a PlacementBinding. The PolicyGenerator solves this. It is a Kustomize generator plugin that takes plain manifests and wraps them for you.

The plugin is not part of the OpenShift GitOps images. An init container copies it from an ACM image into the repo-server, and Kustomize must be allowed to run alpha plugins.

The setup is described in the ACM documentation: ACM 2.17: Accessing the Policy Generator from OpenShift GitOps.

ArgoCD resource on the hub with the PolicyGenerator plugin (excerpt)
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1beta1
kind: ArgoCD
metadata:
  name: policy-gitops
  namespace: policy-gitops
spec:
  kustomizeBuildOptions: --enable-alpha-plugins (1)
  repo:
    env:
      - name: KUSTOMIZE_PLUGIN_HOME
        value: /etc/kustomize/plugin
    initContainers:
      - name: policy-generator-install
        image: registry.redhat.io/rhacm2/multicluster-operators-subscription-rhel9:v2.17 (2)
        command:
          - /bin/bash
        args:
          - -c
          - cp /policy-generator/PolicyGenerator-not-fips-compliant /policy-generator-tmp/PolicyGenerator (3)
        volumeMounts:
          - mountPath: /policy-generator-tmp
            name: policy-generator
    volumeMounts:
      - mountPath: /etc/kustomize/plugin/policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1/policygenerator
        name: policy-generator
    volumes:
      - name: policy-generator
        emptyDir: {}
1 Allows Kustomize to execute the generator plugin.
2 The tag must match the minor version of your ACM hub (oc get multiclusterhub -n open-cluster-management -o jsonpath='{.items[0].status.currentVersion}'). Update it after every hub upgrade, or let a policy do it (see Keeping the image tag in sync).
3 Copies the plugin from the image to the plugin directory.

If your policy folders contain Helm charts that should be rendered before the policies are generated, add the environment variable POLICY_GEN_ENABLE_HELM with the value "true" to spec.repo.env.

Keeping the image tag in sync

A fixed tag has one weakness: after a hub upgrade, the PolicyGenerator in the repo-server is still the old one until somebody updates the tag. The ACM documentation provides an example of a policy that keeps the image tag in sync. After an upgrade of the hub, the policy changes the image of the init container automatically.

The policy runs on the hub only, so it needs a Placement for local-cluster. The hub carries the label local-cluster=true, and it is part of the cluster set global, which must be bound to the policy namespace:

Policy that keeps the PolicyGenerator image in sync with the hub
apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta2
kind: ManagedClusterSetBinding
metadata:
  name: global
  namespace: acm-policies
spec:
  clusterSet: global (1)
---
apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
kind: Policy
metadata:
  name: argocd-policy-generator
  namespace: acm-policies
  annotations:
    policy.open-cluster-management.io/standards: NIST SP 800-53
    policy.open-cluster-management.io/categories: CM Configuration Management
    policy.open-cluster-management.io/controls: CM-2 Baseline Configuration
spec:
  remediationAction: enforce (2)
  disabled: false
  policy-templates:
    - objectDefinition:
        apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
        kind: ConfigurationPolicy
        metadata:
          name: argocd-policy-generator
        spec:
          severity: medium
          object-templates:
            - complianceType: musthave
              objectDefinition:
                apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1beta1
                kind: ArgoCD
                metadata:
                  name: policy-gitops
                  namespace: policy-gitops
                spec:
                  kustomizeBuildOptions: --enable-alpha-plugins
                  repo:
                    env:
                      - name: KUSTOMIZE_PLUGIN_HOME
                        value: /etc/kustomize/plugin
                    initContainers:
                      - name: policy-generator-install
                        image: '{{ (index (lookup "apps/v1" "Deployment" "open-cluster-management" "multicluster-operators-hub-subscription").spec.template.spec.containers 0).image }}' (3)
                        command:
                          - /bin/bash
                        args:
                          - -c
                          - cp /policy-generator/PolicyGenerator-not-fips-compliant /policy-generator-tmp/PolicyGenerator
                        volumeMounts:
                          - mountPath: /policy-generator-tmp
                            name: policy-generator
                    volumeMounts:
                      - mountPath: /etc/kustomize/plugin/policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1/policygenerator
                        name: policy-generator
                    volumes:
                      - name: policy-generator
                        emptyDir: {}
---
apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta1
kind: Placement
metadata:
  name: hub-only
  namespace: acm-policies
spec:
  clusterSets:
    - global
  predicates:
    - requiredClusterSelector:
        labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            local-cluster: "true" (4)
---
apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
kind: PlacementBinding
metadata:
  name: argocd-policy-generator
  namespace: acm-policies
placementRef:
  apiGroup: cluster.open-cluster-management.io
  kind: Placement
  name: hub-only
subjects:
  - apiGroup: policy.open-cluster-management.io
    kind: Policy
    name: argocd-policy-generator
1 The cluster set global contains every managed cluster, including the hub. The Placement below narrows it down to the hub. Creating a ManagedClusterSetBinding requires the permissions managedclustersetbindings and managedclustersets/bind, which are not part of the ClusterRole above. Create it once as cluster administrator, or extend the ClusterRole if Argo CD shall sync it.
2 We enforce this policy.
3 lookup reads the deployment of the ACM subscription controller, and the template takes the image of its first container. That is exactly the image the init container needs, in the version of the running hub.
4 ACM sets this label on the hub’s own ManagedCluster.

Two things to keep in mind:

  • Write this policy as plain YAML, not as PolicyGenerator input. It installs the generator, so it cannot depend on it (hen-egg problem). Argo CD can sync it from Git without the plugin.

  • One owner per object. The policy now manages the plugin part of the ArgoCD resource policy-gitops. If that resource is also deployed by Argo CD (for example, from a Helm chart for OpenShift GitOps), remove the plugin settings from there, or the two will overwrite each other.

Policy health in Argo CD

By default, Argo CD considers a policy healthy as soon as it exists. That is not very useful: you want to see in Argo CD whether the policy is compliant. The policy collection of the Open Cluster Management project contains a policy that adds the matching health checks (resourceHealthChecks) to the ArgoCD resource: argocd-policy-healthchecks.yaml. The policy adds the health checks to every ArgoCD instance it finds on the cluster, so policy-gitops is covered as well. It is shipped with remediationAction: inform: set it to enforce, otherwise it only reports the missing health checks. After that, Argo CD shows a non-compliant policy as Degraded.

Pattern A: policies as code

Pattern A is the governance part of the integration: the policies live in Git, Argo CD on the hub brings them into the cluster, and ACM does the rest. You never create a policy in the ACM console or with oc apply again. Every change is a pull request, and the history of your compliance is stored in Git.

The example in this section builds two policies that show both sides of a policy:

  • service-mesh installs Red Hat OpenShift Service Mesh 3 on the selected clusters: the Operator and a control plane. It is enforced and the manifests are applied in a fixed order, because the control plane resources can only be created after the Operator has installed its CRDs.

  • no-kubeadmin checks that the kubeadmin secret does not exist anymore. It only informs: ACM reports every cluster where the secret is still present, but nothing is deleted automatically.

Both start as plain Kubernetes manifests in Git. The PolicyGenerator wraps them into Policy, Placement and PlacementBinding, so you do not have to write the policy structure yourself.

This requires the hub Argo CD instance policy-gitops with the PolicyGenerator plugin, as described in the previous section.

The following diagram shows the complete flow, from Git to the compliance status in ACM and Argo CD:

Policies as code: from plain manifests in Git to compliance on every cluster

What happens under the hood:

  1. The hub Argo CD renders the policies from Git and syncs them to the hub.

  2. The result is a set of Policy, Placement and PlacementBinding objects in the namespace acm-policies.

  3. ACM creates a replicated policy in the namespace of every selected cluster on the hub.

  4. The policy framework on each managed cluster pulls its replicated policy, evaluates it and, in enforce mode, fixes what is different.

  5. The compliance status flows back to the hub and shows up in the ACM governance view, per policy and cluster.

  6. With the policy health checks, Argo CD shows a non-compliant policy as Degraded.

Repository layout

acm-policies/
├── kustomization.yaml
├── policy-generator.yaml
└── input
    ├── service-mesh
    │   ├── 01-subscription.yaml       # OpenShift Service Mesh 3 Operator
    │   ├── 02-namespace-istio-system.yaml
    │   ├── 03-namespace-istio-cni.yaml
    │   ├── 04-istiocni.yaml           # CNI plugin, required on OpenShift
    │   └── 05-istio.yaml              # the control plane
    └── no-kubeadmin
        └── kubeadmin-secret.yaml

The files in input/ are plain Kubernetes manifests, exactly as you would apply them with oc apply. The Operator is installed in the namespace openshift-operators, which already has an OperatorGroup for all namespaces, so neither a namespace nor an OperatorGroup is needed for it:

input/service-mesh/01-subscription.yaml
apiVersion: operators.coreos.com/v1alpha1
kind: Subscription
metadata:
  name: servicemeshoperator3
  namespace: openshift-operators
spec:
  channel: stable-3.4 (1)
  installPlanApproval: Automatic
  name: servicemeshoperator3
  source: redhat-operators
  sourceNamespace: openshift-marketplace
1 Pins the minor version. Use stable to always get the latest version.

The control plane consists of two cluster-scoped resources, IstioCNI and Istio, each pointing to its own namespace (istio-cni and istio-system):

input/service-mesh/04-istiocni.yaml
apiVersion: sailoperator.io/v1
kind: IstioCNI
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  namespace: istio-cni
input/service-mesh/05-istio.yaml
apiVersion: sailoperator.io/v1
kind: Istio
metadata:
  name: default
spec:
  namespace: istio-system

And the kubeadmin secret that must not exist:

if your original kubeadmin secret is still present, you can ignore this yaml. Honestly, I am not even sure if this would work, once you have removed the secret.
input/no-kubeadmin/kubeadmin-secret.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: kubeadmin
  namespace: kube-system

The kustomization.yaml only references the generator:

kustomization.yaml
generators:
  - policy-generator.yaml

Render the folder locally before you push. If it does not render on your machine, it will not render in Argo CD either. With the PolicyGenerator binary in your Kustomize plugin path:

kustomize build --enable-alpha-plugins acm-policies/

The output contains a Policy, a Placement and a PlacementBinding per policy.

The PolicyGenerator configuration

The file policy-generator.yaml is the heart of the setup. It does not contain any policy itself, it only describes which policies the generator shall create from the manifests in input/. It has two parts:

  • policyDefaults apply to every policy: the namespace on the hub where the policies are created, the default remediation action and severity, and the Placement that decides which clusters receive them.

  • policies lists the policies, each with its name, the manifests it contains and the settings that differ from the defaults.

For every entry in policies, the generator creates a Policy, a Placement and a PlacementBinding. The manifests are wrapped into a ConfigurationPolicy inside the Policy: by default all manifests of a policy into one, with consolidateManifests: false one per manifest. Our two policies use this as follows: service-mesh overrides the defaults to enforce and to apply its manifests in order, while no-kubeadmin keeps the defaults and only changes the compliance type.

policy-generator.yaml
apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
kind: PolicyGenerator
metadata:
  name: cluster-baseline
policyDefaults:
  namespace: acm-policies
  remediationAction: inform (1)
  severity: medium
  placement:
    labelSelector:
      matchExpressions:
        - key: name (5)
          operator: In
          values:
            - sno
            - bm
policies:
  - name: service-mesh
    remediationAction: enforce (2)
    orderManifests: true (3)
    consolidateManifests: false
    manifests:
      - path: input/service-mesh/01-subscription.yaml
      - path: input/service-mesh/02-namespace-istio-system.yaml
      - path: input/service-mesh/03-namespace-istio-cni.yaml
      - path: input/service-mesh/04-istiocni.yaml
      - path: input/service-mesh/05-istio.yaml
  - name: no-kubeadmin
    manifests:
      - path: input/no-kubeadmin/
        complianceType: mustnothave (4)
1 Default for all policies: report only.
2 This policy is enforced.
3 Creates one ConfigurationPolicy per manifest and makes each one depend on the previous one: first the Subscription, then the namespaces, then IstioCNI and Istio. Note that the Subscription policy is compliant as soon as the Subscription exists, not when the Operator is installed. Until the CRDs are there, the IstioCNI policy reports an error and is evaluated again. If you want to wait for the installed Operator, use an OperatorPolicy instead of the Subscription, as shown in Pattern B.
4 The kubeadmin secret must not exist. In inform mode, ACM reports every cluster where it still exists. Remove it with care, only after an identity provider is configured.
5 Selects the clusters sno and bm. ACM sets the label name on every ManagedCluster. For a growing fleet, a label such as environment=production or the cluster set label cluster.open-cluster-management.io/clusterset scales better than a list of names.

Bind the cluster sets to the policy namespace

A Placement only sees the clusters of cluster sets that are bound to its own namespace. The bindings from Ep.19 live in openshift-gitops, so the Placements in acm-policies would find no cluster at all. ACM then shows the warning "ClusterSets failed to load. Verify that there is at least one ClusterSet bound to your selected namespace."

Bind the cluster set production to acm-policies, and global as well if you use the policy that keeps the PolicyGenerator image in sync (its Placement selects the hub from global):

ManagedClusterSetBindings in the policy namespace
apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta2
kind: ManagedClusterSetBinding
metadata:
  name: production
  namespace: acm-policies
spec:
  clusterSet: production
---
apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta2
kind: ManagedClusterSetBinding
metadata:
  name: global
  namespace: acm-policies
spec:
  clusterSet: global

The generated Placements select sno and bm by name, from the cluster sets bound to acm-policies. Check the result:

oc get placementdecisions -n acm-policies \
  -o custom-columns=NAME:.metadata.name,CLUSTERS:.status.decisions[*].clusterName

The Argo CD Application

On the hub, one Application syncs the folder:

Application for the policies
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: acm-policies
  namespace: policy-gitops (1)
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/tjungbauer/acm-policies.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: .
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
    namespace: acm-policies
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: true
      selfHeal: true
1 The Application belongs to the instance policy-gitops. No CreateNamespace=true: the namespace acm-policies already exists with the managed-by label.

Replicated policies

When ACM propagates a policy, it creates a copy in the namespace of every managed cluster on the hub, the replicated policy. Argo CD could treat these copies as extraneous resources of the Application and show it as OutOfSync or even try to delete them. ACM prevents that: it automatically sets the annotation argocd.argoproj.io/compare-options: IgnoreExtraneous on every replicated policy.

Pattern B: a policy bootstraps Argo CD

The bootstrap question from Ep.18: who installs Argo CD on a new cluster? With ACM, the answer is a policy. As soon as a cluster is imported and matches the Placement of the policy, the policy installs OpenShift GitOps and creates a root Application that points to the cluster’s folder in Git. From there, Argo CD configures the rest.

Bootstrap policy: the templates are applied in order, then the local Argo CD takes over

We extend our repository with:

acm-policies/
└── input
    └── gitops-bootstrap
        ├── 01-namespace.yaml          # openshift-gitops-operator
        ├── 02-operatorpolicy.yaml     # OpenShift GitOps Operator
        ├── 03-controller-rbac.yaml    # rights for the local controller
        ├── 04-repo-credentials.yaml   # Git credentials, copied from the hub
        └── 05-root-application.yaml   # app-of-apps for this cluster

The first file creates the namespace for the Operator. The OperatorPolicy in the next step expects it to exist:

input/gitops-bootstrap/01-namespace.yaml
apiVersion: v1
kind: Namespace
metadata:
  name: openshift-gitops-operator
input/gitops-bootstrap/02-operatorpolicy.yaml
apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta1
kind: OperatorPolicy (1)
metadata:
  name: openshift-gitops-operator
spec:
  remediationAction: enforce
  severity: high
  complianceType: musthave
  subscription:
    name: openshift-gitops-operator
    namespace: openshift-gitops-operator
    channel: gitops-1.22 (2)
    source: redhat-operators
    sourceNamespace: openshift-marketplace
  upgradeApproval: Automatic
1 The PolicyGenerator adds OperatorPolicy manifests unchanged as a policy template, no extra wrapping.
2 Pin the channel. Moving to the next version is a one-line pull request.

The root Application is the app-of-apps that contains the Application for every cluster.

input/gitops-bootstrap/05-root-application.yaml
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: Application
metadata:
  name: root
  namespace: openshift-gitops
spec:
  project: default
  source:
    repoURL: https://github.com/tjungbauer/openshift-clusterconfig-gitops.git
    targetRevision: main
    path: '{{hub printf "clusters/%s/bootstrap" .ManagedClusterName hub}}' (1)
  destination:
    server: https://kubernetes.default.svc
  syncPolicy:
    automated:
      prune: false (2)
      selfHeal: true
1 A hub template, resolved on the hub for every cluster: sno gets clusters/sno/bootstrap.
2 Never prune on the root Application. A broken path would otherwise remove everything below it.

The local Argo CD must be allowed to create whatever the root Application brings in. 03-controller-rbac.yaml grants its application-controller cluster-admin rights, the same as in the pull model of Ep.19:

input/gitops-bootstrap/03-controller-rbac.yaml
apiVersion: rbac.authorization.k8s.io/v1
kind: ClusterRoleBinding
metadata:
  name: argo-admin
subjects:
  - kind: ServiceAccount
    name: openshift-gitops-argocd-application-controller (1)
    namespace: openshift-gitops
roleRef:
  apiGroup: rbac.authorization.k8s.io
  kind: ClusterRole
  name: cluster-admin (2)
1 The service account of the default instance openshift-gitops, which the Operator creates after the installation.
2 Simple and usually fine for platform configuration. For application teams, prefer namespaces labelled with argocd.argoproj.io/managed-by.

And the generator configuration ties it together:

policy-generator.yaml (excerpt)
policies:
  - name: gitops-bootstrap
    remediationAction: enforce
    orderManifests: true (1)
    consolidateManifests: false
    placement:
      labelSelector:
        matchExpressions:
          - key: name (2)
            operator: In
            values:
              - sno
              - bm
    manifests:
      - path: input/gitops-bootstrap/01-namespace.yaml
      - path: input/gitops-bootstrap/02-operatorpolicy.yaml
      - path: input/gitops-bootstrap/03-controller-rbac.yaml
      - path: input/gitops-bootstrap/04-repo-credentials.yaml
      - path: input/gitops-bootstrap/05-root-application.yaml
1 The order matters: the Application CRD only exists after the operator is installed. With orderManifests, the root Application is only created when the operator policy is compliant.
2 The same selection as for the other policies: the clusters sno and bm, selected by the name label that ACM sets on every ManagedCluster. In a larger fleet, a dedicated label such as gitops=enabled makes the bootstrap an opt-in per cluster.
Pattern B is meant for clusters that get their Argo CD from this policy. If you followed the pull or agent part of Ep.19, the GitOps add-on of ACM has already installed OpenShift GitOps on sno and bm, and the policy and the add-on would then manage the same operator. Decide which of the two owns the operator before you enforce this policy, or test Pattern B on a cluster without the add-on.

Who owns what afterwards? The policy owns exactly five objects: the namespace, the operator, the ClusterRoleBinding, the repository secret and the root Application. Everything the root Application brings in belongs to Argo CD. Keep it that way: if you also manage the OpenShift GitOps Subscription with Argo CD on the spoke, the two will fight.

The result in ACM & Argo CD

Once Argo CD has synced the repository, the policies show up in the ACM console under Governance.

The list of Policies shows the three policies of this article in the namespace acm-policies: service-mesh, no-kubeadmin and gitops-bootstrap. For each policy you see the remediation action (inform or enforce), the cluster violations and the policy set, if there is one.

Figure 1. Policies in the namespace acm-policies

A click on a policy opens the details. The Details tab shows the policy templates, here the ConfigurationPolicies and the OperatorPolicy that the PolicyGenerator created from the plain manifests, and the Placement with the selected clusters sno and bm.

The no-kubeadmin policy is a good example for inform: ACM only reports that the secret kubeadmin still exists, it does not delete it.

Figure 2. Results of the policy no-kubeadmin

In the Argo CD UI we can also verify the status (including the resource tree).

The Application acm-policies shows the status Degraded. This is because the policy no-kubeadmin is non-compliant …​ the secrets are still present.

Figure 3. Application acm-policies in Argo CD

The resource tree proves this:

Figure 4. Resource tree of the application acm-policies

Summary

That concludes the mini-series. ACM decides where and checks compliance, Argo CD decides what and keeps it in sync, and Git is the only place where changes are made.

And as always: If it is not in Git, it does not exist. That includes your ACM policies.

The diagrams in this article have been manually drawn on a whiteboard. AI then generated the SVGs from photos and made them look equal in all articles.

  • ACM 2.17: Governance (Policy Generator, OperatorPolicy, hub templates)

  • Open Cluster Management: policy collection

item.title: [Ep.18] OpenShift GitOps or Advanced Cluster Management? Choosing the right tool
item.dc:creator: Articles by Thomas Jungbauer
item.description: Compare OpenShift GitOps and Advanced Cluster Management: what each tool does, where they overlap, how they work together and when to choose which.
item.content:encoded:
At customer engagements where I support the implementation of a GitOps process, I often hear the question: "Should we use OpenShift GitOps (Argo CD) or Advanced Cluster Management (Open Cluster Management)?" The honest answer is: it is the wrong question. Both tools solve different problems, they overlap in one specific area, and in larger environments with numerous clusters they are designed to work together.

In this article I will try to explain what each tool is (and also what it is not), where they overlap, how they integrate, and I will walk through an example, so that you can decide for yourself which tool fits which job.

The topic turned out to be too big for a single article, so I have split it into multiple parts and maybe I should have split into even more. This is the first:

  1. [Ep.18] OpenShift GitOps or Advanced Cluster Management? (this article): what each tool does, where they overlap and a decision guide.

  2. [Ep.19] ACM and OpenShift GitOps: push, pull and the Argo CD Agent: how ACM registers clusters in Argo CD, and how to set up each of the three delivery models.

  3. [Ep.20] Managing ACM Policies with OpenShift GitOps: policies as code, the PolicyGenerator, hub templates and bootstrapping Argo CD with a policy.

Everything in this series was written against OpenShift GitOps 1.22 (Argo CD 3.5) and Advanced Cluster Management 2.17 (Open Cluster Management). Technology Preview and GA states move quickly in both products, so check the release notes of your versions before you commit to a design.
While I am using the term "Advanced Cluster Management" in this article, I am referring to the product formerly known as Open Cluster Management. Same counts for Argo CD and OpenShift GitOps.

The short answer

  • OpenShift GitOps (Argo CD) answers the question: "Is the state in Git the state on my cluster(s)?" It is a delivery engine.

  • Advanced Cluster Management (ACM) answers the question: "Which clusters do I have, how are they doing, and do they comply with my rules?" It is a fleet management platform.

  • ACM does not replace Argo CD. For application delivery, ACM uses OpenShift GitOps. What ACM adds is the knowledge about the fleet: which clusters exist, which labels they carry, which ones are healthy.

  • The real overlap is cluster configuration: you can configure clusters with Argo CD Applications or with ACM Policies. Choose what fits best, and never let both tools manage the same object.

Or, in one sentence I like to use with customers: ACM decides where and checks compliance. Argo CD decides what and keeps it in sync.

Other features ACM offers are an automated cluster deployment and centralized observability. But these are not the focus of this article.

What OpenShift GitOps is

OpenShift GitOps is Red Hat’s distribution of Argo CD, delivered and lifecycle-managed by the OpenShift GitOps Operator. It is included in the OpenShift subscription. At the time of writing, the current version is 1.22, which ships Argo CD 3.5. New releases and features come quickly, always check the release notes of your version first.

The core job of Argo CD is reconciliation: it renders manifests (plain YAML, Kustomize, Helm, etc.), compares them with the live state of a cluster and syncs differences. Everything else (ApplicationSets, sync waves, hooks, RBAC via AppProjects, the UI) is built around that job.

If you want to dig into the details of the GitOps process, Ep.1 is a good introduction to the topic.

What OpenShift GitOps does not do:

  • It does not create, upgrade, or destroy clusters. A cluster has to exist, and someone has to register it in Argo CD.

  • It does not report compliance. It tells you that an (Argo CD) Application is Synced and Healthy. It does not tell you that three out of 40 clusters violate your NIST 800-53 baseline.

  • It has no fleet-wide view of anything that is not an Argo CD Application: no search across clusters, no metrics, no inventory.

That is perfectly fine. Argo CD was never meant to do any of these things.

What Advanced Cluster Management is

Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management for Kubernetes is a hub-and-spoke platform. You install it on a hub cluster and import or create managed clusters. It is a separate subscription, or part of OpenShift Platform Plus. At the time of writing, the current version is 2.17. The open source equivalent is called Open Cluster Management.

ACM is built around five pillars:

Pillar What it does

Cluster lifecycle (multicluster engine)

Create, import, upgrade, and destroy clusters: Installer Provided Infrastructure (IPI) on cloud providers, Hosted Control Planes, Assisted/Agent-based installs on bare metal, ROSA/ARO, import clusters and so on.

Governance

Policies that check (inform) or enforce configuration on managed clusters, with compliance status reported back to the hub. Integrates with Gatekeeper, the Compliance Operator and certificate checks.

Application lifecycle

Deploy applications to many clusters. It uses Argo CD in the background for this task.

Observability

Centralized metrics and Grafana dashboards across the fleet.

Search and fleet views

Search any resource across all managed clusters, including a dedicated view for virtual machines from OpenShift Virtualization.

The building blocks you will meet everywhere in ACM are:

  • ManagedCluster – the cluster that is managed, the representation of a spoke on the hub, carrying labels (for example environment=production, region=eu-central).

  • ManagedClusterSet – a group of clusters, used for RBAC and scoping.

  • ManagedClusterSetBinding – makes a cluster set usable from a namespace on the hub.

  • Placement – a dynamic selection of clusters based on labels, etc. It defines the scope of a policy or application.

Below is a more detailed description of the different objects

The Placement is the important concept for this series. Argo CD selects clusters by looking at labels on cluster secrets that someone created. ACM selects clusters by looking at the actual fleet, including whether a cluster is available right now.

ACM also has its own, older application model based on Channels and Subscriptions objects. That model is deprecated and will be removed in a future release.

Side-by-side comparison

Let’s do a side-by-side comparison of the two tools:

Topic OpenShift GitOps Advanced Cluster Management

Primary purpose

Continuous delivery from Git

Fleet management: lifecycle, governance, visibility

Scope

One or more clusters, registered manually

Hundreds or thousands of managed clusters

Cluster creation and upgrades

No (cluster upgrades only via a ClusterVersion manifest, see Ep.10)

Yes (including upgrades with pre/post hooks)

Source of truth

Git (or Helm/OCI repository)

The hub cluster. The hub objects themselves can (and should) come from Git, so maybe it is still Git after all.

Configuration management

Applications, ApplicationSets

Policies (ConfigurationPolicy, OperatorPolicy, …​)

"Inform only" / audit mode

Partly, shows OutOfSync of managed resources

Yes (remediationAction: inform)

Compliance reporting

No

Yes, per policy, per cluster, with history

Per-cluster templating

ApplicationSet generators, Helm values

Hub templates and managed-cluster templates in policies

Behaviour when the hub is unreachable

Push model: nothing is reconciled. Agent/pull model: local reconciliation continues

Policies keep being evaluated and enforced on the managed cluster

Licensing

Included in OpenShift. Clusters running the Argo CD Agent need OpenShift Platform Plus

Separate subscription or OpenShift Platform Plus

Who does what in a combined setup

When both tools are in place, the question is no longer "which one", but "which one for which task". This is the split I would like to recommend:

Area ACM Argo CD

Cluster lifecycle

Create, import, upgrade, hibernate

–

Fleet inventory and selection

ManagedCluster labels, ManagedClusterSets, Placements

Consumes them (GitOpsCluster, cluster decision generator)

Governance / Compliance

Policies (inform/enforce), compliance history

Deploys the policies from Git to the hub. Can show health status.

Cluster configuration

Possible with ConfigurationPolicies

Preferred: richer diff, sync waves, health

Application delivery

Placement of Applications, pull transport

The delivery engine (push, pull, agent)

Observability

Multicluster observability, search

Sync and health status only

Bootstrapping Argo CD on new clusters

Policy or GitOps add-on installs it everywhere

–

Where they overlap: cluster configuration

While application deployment is clearly the responsibility of Argo CD, creating new clusters or upgrading existing ones is clearly ACM territory. The grey zone is cluster configuration: Operators, OAuth, RBAC, network policies, the compliance baseline. Both tools can do it, but you should choose what fits best.

To make the difference visible, let’s implement the same requirement twice:

"Every production cluster must run the Compliance Operator from the stable channel."

Option 1: Argo CD with an ApplicationSet

Without ACM, Argo CD needs to know the target clusters. That means a cluster secret per cluster, carrying the labels we want to select on and the token to access the cluster:

Cluster secret for a production cluster
apiVersion: v1
kind: Secret
metadata:
  name: cluster-prod-eu-01
  namespace: openshift-gitops
  labels:
    argocd.argoproj.io/secret-type: cluster (1)
    environment: production (2)
type: Opaque
stringData:
  name: prod-eu-01
  server: https://api.prod-eu-01.example.com:6443
  config: | (3)
    {
      "bearerToken": "<token-of-a-service-account-on-the-spoke>",
      "tlsClientConfig": {
        "insecure": false,
        "caData": "<base64-encoded-ca>"
      }
    }
1 Marks this secret as a cluster definition for Argo CD.
2 Our own label. The ApplicationSet uses it for the selection.
3 Access configuration for the cluster.

The ApplicationSet then uses the cluster generator to create one Application per matching cluster:

Other generators are available too, but for simplicity only the cluster generator is used here.
ApplicationSet with cluster generator
apiVersion: argoproj.io/v1alpha1
kind: ApplicationSet
metadata:
  name: compliance-operator
  namespace: openshift-gitops
spec:
  goTemplate: true
  goTemplateOptions: ["missingkey=error"]
  generators:
    - clusters:
        selector:
          matchLabels:
            environment: production (1)
  template:
    metadata:
      name: 'compliance-operator-{{ .name }}'
    spec:
      project: default
      source:
        repoURL: https://github.com/tjungbauer/openshift-clusterconfig-gitops.git
        targetRevision: main
        path: clusters/all/setup-compliance-operator
      destination:
        server: '{{ .server }}' (2)
      syncPolicy:
        automated:
          prune: true
          selfHeal: true
1 Selects all cluster secrets with this label.
2 Argo CD on the hub pushes the manifests directly to the API of each spoke.

This works well and it is exactly what I do in my own demo environment. The catch is in the details:

  • The token in the cluster secret must be created, rotated and stored securely. For 5 clusters that is fine, for 200 clusters it is a project of its own.

  • The hub needs network access to the API of every spoke.

  • Whoever controls this Argo CD instance effectively has the permissions of every token it holds.

  • The result is "Synced/Healthy". There is no compliance report you can hand to an auditor.

Option 2: ACM with an OperatorPolicy

With ACM, the same requirement is a policy. A Placement selects the clusters, a PlacementBinding connects the policy with the Placement:

Policy, Placement and PlacementBinding
apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
kind: Policy
metadata:
  name: compliance-operator
  namespace: acm-policies
  annotations:
    policy.open-cluster-management.io/standards: NIST SP 800-53
    policy.open-cluster-management.io/categories: CM Configuration Management
    policy.open-cluster-management.io/controls: CM-2 Baseline Configuration
spec:
  disabled: false
  remediationAction: enforce (1)
  policy-templates:
    - objectDefinition:
        apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
        kind: ConfigurationPolicy (2)
        metadata:
          name: compliance-operator-namespace
        spec:
          severity: high
          object-templates:
            - complianceType: musthave
              objectDefinition:
                apiVersion: v1
                kind: Namespace
                metadata:
                  name: openshift-compliance
    - objectDefinition:
        apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta1
        kind: OperatorPolicy (3)
        metadata:
          name: compliance-operator
        spec:
          severity: high
          complianceType: musthave
          subscription:
            name: compliance-operator
            namespace: openshift-compliance
            channel: stable
            source: redhat-operators
            sourceNamespace: openshift-marketplace
          upgradeApproval: Automatic (4)
---
apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta1
kind: Placement
metadata:
  name: production-clusters
  namespace: acm-policies
spec:
  clusterSets:
    - production (5)
  predicates:
    - requiredClusterSelector:
        labelSelector:
          matchLabels:
            environment: production
---
apiVersion: policy.open-cluster-management.io/v1
kind: PlacementBinding (6)
metadata:
  name: compliance-operator
  namespace: acm-policies
placementRef:
  name: production-clusters
  apiGroup: cluster.open-cluster-management.io
  kind: Placement
subjects:
  - name: compliance-operator
    apiGroup: policy.open-cluster-management.io
    kind: Policy
1 Set this to inform and ACM only reports whether the clusters comply, without changing anything.
2 A ConfigurationPolicy ensures that an object exists (musthave), matches exactly (mustonlyhave) or does not exist (mustnothave).
3 The OperatorPolicy handles the OLM details: OperatorGroup, Subscription, install plan approval and the health of the CSV.
4 Controls whether new versions are approved automatically. With None, ACM does not approve upgrades. With spec.complianceConfig, the policy can additionally report available upgrades, since ACM 2.17 even minor version upgrades on other channels.
5 The Placement can only see clusters of cluster sets that are bound to the namespace acm-policies via a ManagedClusterSetBinding (see below).
6 The PlacementBinding connects the policy with the Placement.
One important difference to Argo CD I maybe should have mentioned earlier: Argo CD can manage objects it knows. It has no concept of "delete an object completely that cannot compare with Git". For example, delete the secret "kubeadmin". ACM is able to do that, you can create a policy that ensures the secret is deleted.

The ManagedClusterSetBinding mentioned in callout 5 looks like the following. It binds the cluster set production to the namespace acm-policies.

apiVersion: cluster.open-cluster-management.io/v1beta2
kind: ManagedClusterSetBinding (1)
metadata:
  name: production
  namespace: acm-policies
spec:
  clusterSet: production
1 The ManagedClusterSetBinding binds the cluster set production to the namespace acm-policies.

Object model of ACM together with Argo CD

Even after working with ACM for a while, I still find it difficult to understand the object model or to explain it to others. Therefore, I tried to create a visual representation of the objects and their relationships here, to help you to understand and to remind myself when I forget. :)

How do these objects play together? The easiest way to understand it is to follow a few clusters through the chain. In the following example, four clusters are imported into ACM. Each step narrows the selection down:

  1. Every imported cluster is a ManagedCluster on the hub. The labels are what everything else selects on.

  2. The ManagedClusterSet production groups clusters. dev-eu-01 belongs to another cluster set and is ignored.

  3. The ManagedClusterSetBinding makes the cluster set usable in a namespace, here openshift-gitops. Without this binding, a Placement in that namespace does not find a single cluster, which is the most common reason for an empty selection.

  4. The Placement selects from the bound cluster sets only. It asks for environment=prod, so prod-eu-02 (a test cluster) is ignored as well.

  5. The PlacementDecision is the result: prod-eu-01 and prod-us-01. ACM keeps it up to date when clusters join, leave or change their labels.

Figure 1. How ACM selects clusters: from ManagedCluster to PlacementDecision

The PlacementDecision itself does not deploy anything. It is just a list and the point where it is handed over to the consumers (Argo CD). Other objects in the same namespace read it and act on it:

  • The GitOpsCluster registers the selected managed clusters automatically in Argo CD by creating a cluster secret for each of them. ACM rotates the tokens automatically, therefore you do not need to take care of that.

  • An ApplicationSet creates one Application per selected cluster and uses these cluster secrets as destinations.

  • For governance, a PlacementBinding connects a Policy with a Placement. ACM then puts a copy of the Policy into the hub namespace of each selected cluster, where it gets picked up.

Clusters that are not part of the decision receive nothing: no Application, no Policy.

Figure 2. What uses the PlacementDecision
Consumers can only reference a Placement in their own namespace. Policies usually live in a different namespace (for example acm-policies), so they need their own ManagedClusterSetBinding and Placement there, typically with the same selection.

What is the advantage now?

So after all these different objects and relationships, which look rather complex at the beginning, what is the advantage of ACM?

  • No extra credentials per cluster: the managed clusters are already registered with the hub. The policy is pulled by the policy addon on the spoke and evaluated locally. ACM takes care of the tokens automatically.

  • The hub does not need to reach the API of the spoke.

  • If the hub is unreachable, the spoke keeps enforcing the last known policy because it is stored locally. Good for edge clusters with unstable connectivity.

  • A compliance view: "compliance-operator: 37 compliant, 3 non-compliant", with the reason per cluster and a history.

The rule of thumb

  • Applications and everything owned by application teams: → Argo CD.

  • Baseline configuration that must be audited (security settings, mandatory Operators, certificates, "this must never exist"): → ACM Policies.

  • Platform configuration that is complex to render (a full logging stack, a service mesh control plane): → Argo CD, optionally wrapped by an ACM Policy that only checks (inform) the result.

The anti-pattern: two controllers, one object

One thing I have seen more than once: Argo CD manages an object with selfHeal: true, and an ACM policy enforces the same object with a slightly different value. Each controller "fixes" the drift caused by the other one. The object flips back and forth.

Every object must have exactly one owner. If an ACM Policy and Argo CD should both care about an object, let Argo CD own it and use the policy of ACM in inform mode only.

The bootstrap question: who installs Argo CD?

GitOps needs one first imperative step: somebody has to install the OpenShift GitOps Operator and apply the first (root) Application. Everything after that comes from Git. This is also a question where ACM and Argo CD meet:

Approach Good for Watch out

Script or oc apply

PoC, a handful of clusters, workshops

A manual step per cluster. Version and document the script.

Automation (Ansible, Terraform, …​)

Customers with Automation environment

A second tool to maintain. Keep it to the bootstrap only.

Install-time manifests

Repeatable on-premises installations (agent-based installer)

Must tolerate CRD timing until the operator is up.

ACM Policy

Fleets: every imported cluster is bootstrapped automatically

Policy and Argo CD must not fight over the same objects.

ACM GitOpsCluster

Hub Argo CD (push) or GitOps add-on (pull/agent) targets the cluster

The hub becomes part of the critical path.
My recommendation: fewer than five clusters, use a script or Ansible. For a fleet that is managed by ACM, use a policy or the GitOpsCluster. Never: "we click it in the console once". The bootstrap policy is shown in Ep.20.

Working together: ACM as the brain for Argo CD

As mentioned above, ACM can register its managed clusters in OpenShift GitOps automatically. You no longer maintain cluster secrets by hand: ACM creates them, based on a Placement, rotates the credentials automatically and removes the secrets when a cluster is removed from the Placement.

The bridge between the two worlds is the GitOpsCluster custom resource. On top of it, ACM offers three options to get an Argo CD Application onto a managed cluster:

Model How it works Use it when

Push

Argo CD on the hub pushes manifests to the spoke API, like option 1 above. ACM creates and rotates the cluster secrets.

A moderate number of clusters, good connectivity from hub to spokes, and you want one UI with full visibility.

Pull

Applications are created on the hub but not reconciled there. Instead the target cluster pulls it and a local Argo CD instance on the target cluster reconciles it.

Many clusters, outbound-only networks, or the hub must not hold credentials for the spokes.

Argo CD Agent

ACM deploys the Argo CD Agent to the spokes via the GitOps add-on. Applications are defined on the hub, the agent reconciles locally and synchronises the full status back.

The direction for large fleets and edge sites.

The following diagram shows how the three models fit together.

Figure 3. Three ways an Argo CD Application reaches a managed cluster
Yes, you read that right, the version will jump from 2.17 to 5.0 for ACM in the next release, to harmonize with OpenShift versioning.

What each model actually is, how the data flows in which direction and how to set it up step by step is the topic of the next part: [Ep.19] ACM and OpenShift GitOps: push, pull and the Argo CD Agent.

Decision guide

The following are the scenarios I saw in real projects and what I personally would recommend. Verify if these fit your situation.

A quick summary of the scenarios is shown in the following slide I was using for a workshop (more details below):

Figure 4. Decision guide: OpenShift GitOps alone or together with ACM

Scenario A: one to three clusters, one platform team

Example: a single production cluster plus a test cluster.

OpenShift GitOps only. ACM would add a hub, an additional component to operate and additional cost, without solving a real problem. Configure the clusters with Argo CD as described in the earlier episodes of this series, with either one Argo CD instance per cluster or a central Argo CD on a management cluster (recommended). If you need compliance reports, the Compliance Operator gives you scan results per cluster without ACM.

Scenario B: 3 to 20 clusters, all reachable, created by another team or process

Example: dev, test, prod in two data centres, installed by the infrastructure team.

OpenShift GitOps is usually sufficient. A central Argo CD with an ApplicationSet cluster generator, or decentralised Argo CD instances per cluster. Start thinking about ACM when one of these questions comes up:

  • "Who rotates the cluster tokens in the Argo CD secrets?"

  • "Can you show us which clusters are not compliant?"

  • "Can we have one search, one observability view across all clusters?"

Scenario C: 20 to several hundred clusters

Example: clusters per business unit, factory or per tenant, created on demand.

ACM plus OpenShift GitOps. Push for smaller fleets, pull or agent for larger fleets. ACM creates the clusters, labels them and adds them to cluster sets. The GitOpsCluster registers them in Argo CD automatically. Applications and complex platform components come via ApplicationSets driven by ACM Placements. A new cluster receives its full configuration without anybody touching Argo CD. Around 20 clusters is also where a single push hub usually needs sharding, and where the "hub holds all the credentials" discussion with the security team starts. The pull model or the Argo CD Agent become serious options here.

Scenario D: regulated environment

Example: banking or public sector, regular audits, a defined security baseline.

ACM Policies for the baseline, Argo CD for the rest. The baseline lives as policies in Git, deployed by Argo CD to the hub, enforced and reported by ACM. Start in inform mode on existing clusters, check the compliance dashboard, then switch to enforce.

Scenario E: edge and disconnected sites

Example: hundreds of small clusters (SNO, compact clusters) in stores, factories or vehicles with unstable connectivity.

ACM plus OpenShift GitOps in pull or agent mode. The push model fails here: the hub cannot reliably reach the spokes. Policies are evaluated locally and continue to work when the connection is down. Applications are reconciled by a local Argo CD or the Argo CD Agent. Two things to keep in mind: every spoke still needs to reach its sources (Git or an OCI registry, often a local mirror), and every cluster that runs the Argo CD Agent needs an OpenShift Platform Plus subscription.

Frequently asked questions

Just some questions I heard from customers during the last years:

Can ACM replace Argo CD? For applications, no. ACM’s application lifecycle is built on OpenShift GitOps. The older Channel and Subscription model still exists, but it is deprecated. I would not start a new project with Channels and Subscriptions.

Can Argo CD replace ACM? For delivery to existing, reachable clusters, yes. For cluster lifecycle, compliance reporting, fleet search and observability, no.

Do we need ACM to do multi-cluster GitOps? No. Argo CD handles multiple clusters on its own, and with the Argo CD Agent even in a hub-and-spoke model with local reconciliation (see Ep.15). ACM makes it easier to operate at scale, because the cluster registration, the token rotation and the agent installation are automated.

Should the ACM hub itself be managed by Argo CD? Yes. The MultiClusterHub, the policies, Placements, cluster sets, GitOpsCluster resources: all of it belongs in Git. The hub is just another cluster.

Should I configure the cluster with Argo CD or with policies? See the rule of thumb above. And whatever you choose always keep in mind: one owner per object.

Summary

So, which one is better? Neither. They are not competitors, they are layers.

  • OpenShift GitOps is the delivery engine. It makes sure that what is in Git is running on a cluster. It is included in OpenShift and should be your default for applications and complex platform components, no matter how many clusters you have.

  • Advanced Cluster Management is the fleet layer on top. It knows which clusters exist, creates and upgrades them, enforces and reports compliance, and feeds Argo CD with the list of clusters via Placements.

  • The real decision is not "GitOps or ACM", but "do I need fleet management?" For a handful of clusters, usually not. For many clusters, dynamic cluster creation, regulated environments or edge sites, almost certainly yes.

  • Where both tools can do the same job, cluster configuration, use policies for the audited baseline and Argo CD for everything that needs rendering, and keep exactly one owner per object.

In the next part, we look under the hood of the integration: push, pull and the Argo CD Agent.

And as always: If it is not in Git, it does not exist.

The diagrams in this article have been manually drawn on a whiteboard. AI then generated the SVGs from photos and made them look equal in all articles.

References

  • Red Hat OpenShift GitOps 1.22 release notes

  • Red Hat Advanced Cluster Management for Kubernetes 2.17 documentation

  • ACM 2.17: GitOps overview

  • Red Hat blog: Manage clusters and applications at scale with the Argo CD Agent

  • OpenGitOps principles

item.title: The Guide to OpenBao - Authentication Methods - Part 7
item.dc:creator: Articles by Thomas Jungbauer
item.description: Configuring authentication methods in OpenBao including Kubernetes auth, OIDC, LDAP, and AppRole for secure access control
item.content:encoded:
With OpenBao deployed and running, the next critical step is configuring authentication. Ultimately, you want to limit access to only authorised people. This article covers two common authentication methods: Kubernetes for pods and LDAP for enterprise directories (in a simplified example). There are many more methods, but we cannot cover them all in this article.

Introduction

Authentication in OpenBao verifies the identity of clients before granting access to secrets. OpenBao supports multiple authentication methods, each suited for different use cases. Among others it supports:

Method Best For Key Features

Kubernetes

Pods running in K8s/OpenShift

Service account tokens, automatic

OIDC

Human users, SSO

OpenShift OAuth, Keycloak, Azure AD

LDAP

Enterprise directories

Active Directory, OpenLDAP

AppRole

CI/CD, automation

Role ID + Secret ID

Token

Direct access, bootstrap

Simple but less secure
The full documentation of the authentication methods and the list of available methods (for example Radius) can be found here: OpenBao Authentication Methods.

Authentication Workflow

The authentication workflow in OpenBao from a user perspective is as follows:

  1. A client wants to authenticate to OpenBao and provides credentials.

  2. OpenBao validates the credentials against the authentication method. For example: LDAP

  3. If the authentication method (e.g. LDAP) is successful, it will return the required information about the client.

  4. OpenBao maps this result to policies that are mapped to the authentication method.

  5. OpenBao generates a token that is associated with the policies and returns it to the client.

  6. The client can then use this token for further operations.

Prerequisites for Authentication Methods

Before configuring authentication:

  • OpenBao is deployed and unsealed (Parts 2-6)

  • You have admin access to OpenBao (root token)

  • Access to the required authentication backend:

    • For Kubernetes auth: Access to the OpenShift cluster

    • For LDAP: Access to the LDAP server

    • etc.

Set up your environment:

You can set up your environment by using either the CLI or the UI.

Using the CLI

Understanding Policies

Before you can actually use an authentication method, it is important to understand what policies do. A policy is a way to declaratively define what (which paths) authenticated users can access or not. All paths are denied by default. A policy is mapped to an authentication method. For example, when we look at LDAP, we could configure something like this:

Every member of group "dev" is mapped to a policy named "dev-policy". The policy then allows the user to read the secrets under the path "secret/data/dev/*".

Basic Policy Structure

A policy is a set of path rules. Each rule says: “for this path (or path prefix), the bearer of this policy may use these capabilities.” Paths are tied to OpenBao’s internal API: for example, secrets in the KV v2 engine live under secret/data/<mount-path>/<key>, so a path like secret/data/myapp/* means “any key under the myapp prefix in the KV v2 store mounted at secret/.”

The example below does two things that are typical for an application policy:

  1. Secrets access: It allows read and list on secret/data/myapp/*.

    • read lets the client fetch the value of a secret at a path (e.g. secret/data/myapp/database).

    • list is required to list keys under a path (e.g. to discover myapp/database, myapp/api-key); without it, the client would need to know every path in advance.

  2. Token renewal: It allows update on auth/token/renew-self. Tokens often have a limited lifetime; this path lets the holder extend their own token without needing the root token or extra permissions. Including it avoids applications losing access when the token expires.

Policies can be written in JSON or HCL. 
# Example policy: myapp-read-policy.hcl
# Allow reading secrets from specific path (KV v2 engine at mount "secret/")
path "secret/data/myapp/*" {
  capabilities = ["read", "list"]
}

# Allow renewing own token so the app can extend its token before expiry
path "auth/token/renew-self" {
  capabilities = ["update"]
}

The path secret/data/myapp/* assumes you have a KV v2 secrets engine mounted at secret/ and will store application secrets under keys like myapp/database, myapp/api-key, etc. Adjust the mount path and prefix to match your setup.

The use of globs (*) may result in surprising or unexpected behaviour. Use them with caution.

Policy Capabilities

Each path defined in a policy must have at least one capability. This provides control over the allowed or denied operations a user may perform. There are several capabilities available:

  • create - Create new data at the given path

  • read - Read data

  • update - Update existing data

  • patch - Patch existing data (Partial update)

  • delete - Delete data

  • list - List keys at a path

  • scan - Scan or browse the path for keys

  • sudo - Allows access to paths that are root-protected.

  • deny - Explicitly deny (overrides other grants)

Default Policies

When OpenBao is deployed the first time, there are no additional authentication methods enabled, except for token. This is required for the root access itself. To allow the administrator to access using the root token, there is one default policy called root. This policy is somewhat of a catch-all policy; it allows the administrator to access everything.

In addition to the root policy, there is one other default policy called default. This policy is used for all authenticated users. It allows them, for example, to look up their own properties and to renew or revoke their own token.
